reason: The text demonstrates repeated instances of Hebrew ingratitude toward both their leaders and Yahweh. After witnessing God's deliverance from Egypt and the parting of the Red Sea, the Hebrews complain multiple times in the wilderness. At Marah, they murmur against Moses when encountering bitter water (וַיִּלֹּ֧נוּ הָעָ֛ם עַל־ מֹשֶׁ֥ה). In the Sin desert, they express nostalgia for Egyptian slavery, saying they would rather have died in Egypt than face hunger: 'Who will give us meat to eat in the land of Egypt?' (מִֽי־ יִתֵּ֨ן מוּתֵ֤נוּ בְיַד־ יְהוָה֙). At Rephidim, they quarrel with Moses and question God's purpose: 'Why have you brought us up from Egypt to kill us?' (לָ֥מָּה זֶּ֖ה הֶעֱלִיתָ֣נוּ מִמִּצְרַ֔יִם). These complaints reflect a pattern of ingratitude despite witnessing miraculous deliverances and divine provision.
